title: SPARK CSEC Physics - Paper 02 Practice Paper 4
subject: Physics
syllabus: CXC 22/G/SYLL 13, for examinations from May and June 2015
instructions: This paper consists of SIX questions in TWO sections. Answer ALL questions.
Write your answers in the spaces provided in this booklet.
Do NOT write in the margins.
Where appropriate, ALL WORKING MUST BE SHOWN in this booklet.
You may use a silent, non-programmable calculator. Note that an answer given to an inappropriate number of figures will be penalised.
required_materials: Graph paper or an on-screen grid

mark_scheme_key.M: Method mark. Awarded for the right approach and a correct substitution, whether or not the arithmetic that follows is right.
mark_scheme_key.A: Accuracy mark. Awarded for the correct value, with its unit, to the precision asked for. Normally depends on the method mark before it.
mark_scheme_key.B: Independent mark. Stands on its own and depends on nothing earlier: a definition, a named source of error, a labelled axis.

marking_conventions: A correct final answer implies the method, unless the question demanded the working.
Follow through. Where a candidate uses their own wrong value correctly in a later part, mark that later part on their value.
A missing unit is penalised once per question, not once per part.
An answer given to more figures than asked for keeps the mark. An answer with fewer figures than the data justify loses it.

marking_coverage.note: A criterion carrying a `check` is marked automatically. A criterion carrying `manual: true` is for prose, a drawn graph or a completed table, which cannot be judged from a typed string without a keyword list written for that answer. The engine reports a manual criterion as something to check against the worked solution rather than counting it as lost.

provenance: Original questions written for SPARK. The structure, language, mark allocations and question archetypes follow the CSEC Physics Paper 02 papers of 2008 to 2023. No past-paper question is reproduced. This is not a Caribbean Examinations Council publication.

questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 4
questions.stem: A student investigated the upthrust on a metal cylinder as it was lowered into water. The cylinder was hung from a spring balance, as shown in Figure 1. In air the spring balance read 2.00 N. The cylinder was then lowered into the water in steps, and the reading on the spring balance was recorded for each volume of the cylinder below the water surface. The results are shown in Table 1.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State Archimedes' principle, and use it to explain why the reading on the spring balance fell as the cylinder was lowered further into the water.
parts.answer: Archimedes' principle states that when a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, the upthrust on it equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. As more of the cylinder went below the surface it displaced more water, so the upthrust grew, and the spring balance supported less of the cylinder's weight.
parts.solution:

As more of the cylinder went below the surface it displaced more water, so the upthrust grew, and the spring balance supported less of the cylinder's weight.

Marker's note. B1 requires the words weight of fluid displaced. 'The upthrust equals the volume displaced' is dimensionally wrong and scores nothing. For B2 accept any answer which says the upthrust increased, so the balance had less to support.

questions.topic: Scalars, vectors and the resultant of forces

parts.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction. Examples: mass or speed; force or velocity.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by the term 'equilibrium', and state the TWO conditions which must be satisfied if a body acted on by several forces is to be in equilibrium.
parts.answer: A body is in equilibrium when it is at rest, or moving with constant velocity, so that it has no acceleration. The resultant force on it must be zero, and the sum of the clockwise moments about any point must equal the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.
parts.solution:

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain why the bulb of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is made thin-walled, and why the bore of the tube is made narrow.
parts.answer: The bulb is thin-walled so that heat passes quickly through the glass to the liquid, and the thermometer responds quickly. The bore is narrow so that a small change in the volume of the liquid produces a large movement along the tube, making the thermometer more sensitive.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A polythene rod becomes negatively charged when it is rubbed with a woollen cloth. Explain, in terms of the movement of electrons, how this happens, and state the charge left on the cloth.
parts.answer: Rubbing transfers electrons from the wool to the polythene. The polythene gains electrons and so becomes negatively charged. The cloth, having lost electrons, is left with an equal positive charge.
parts.solution:
Rubbing transfers electrons from the wool to the polythene. The polythene gains electrons and so becomes negatively charged. The cloth, having lost electrons, is left with an equal positive charge.

Marker's note. Only electrons move. An answer which says the rod gains a negative charge from the cloth, or that protons move, loses B1. The charges are equal and opposite, which is worth saying but not required.
parts.markerNote: Only electrons move. An answer which says the rod gains a negative charge from the cloth, or that protons move, loses B1. The charges are equal and opposite, which is worth saying but not required.

criteria.description: electrons are transferred from the cloth to the rod

the cloth is left positively charged

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the law of electrostatic charges.
parts.answer: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
parts.solution:
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

Marker's note. Both halves are needed for both marks. Attraction alone does not prove a body is charged, since a charged body also attracts an uncharged one.
parts.markerNote: Both halves are needed for both marks. Attraction alone does not prove a body is charged, since a charged body also attracts an uncharged one.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how an insulated metal sphere may be given a positive charge by induction, using a negatively charged rod.
parts.answer: Bring the negatively charged rod near the sphere without touching it. The electrons in the sphere are repelled to the far side, leaving the near side positive. Earth the far side of the sphere by touching it, so that the repelled electrons flow away to earth. Remove the finger first, then remove the rod, and the sphere is left with an overall positive charge.
parts.solution:
Bring the negatively charged rod near the sphere without touching it. The electrons in the sphere are repelled to the far side, leaving the near side positive. Earth the far side of the sphere by touching it, so that the repelled electrons flow away to earth. Remove the finger first, then remove the rod, and the sphere is left with an overall positive charge.

Marker's note. The order in B4 is the whole point of the method and is the mark most often lost. Removing the rod first lets the electrons flow back and the sphere ends up uncharged. The charge induced is opposite to that on the rod, so a negative rod gives a positive sphere; a candidate who ends with a negative sphere has described charging by contact and loses B2 and B4.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how a lightning conductor protects a tall building.
parts.answer: The conductor is a thick copper strip running from a spike above the building to a plate buried in the ground. The sharp point causes charge to leak away from the building and partly discharge the cloud. If lightning does strike, the conductor carries the very large current safely to earth instead of through the building.

If lightning does strike, the conductor carries the very large current safely to earth instead of through the building.

Marker's note. An answer which says only that the conductor 'attracts the lightning' has half of B3 and does not earn it on its own: the useful part is where the current then goes.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain why a fuel tanker is earthed by a chain or a wire before fuel is pumped from it, and state what could happen if it were not.
parts.answer: Fuel flowing through the pipe rubs against it and charge builds up on the tanker. The chain or wire provides a path to earth so the charge leaks away steadily. Without it the charge could build until a spark jumps, and a spark near fuel vapour could cause an explosion.

Fuel flowing through the pipe rubs against it and charge builds up on the tanker. The chain or wire provides a path to earth so the charge leaks away steadily. Without it the charge could build until a spark jumps, and a spark near fuel vapour could cause an explosion.

Marker's note. B3 must name the spark and the ignition. 'It would be dangerous' scores nothing.
parts.markerNote: B3 must name the spark and the ignition. 'It would be dangerous' scores nothing.

criteria.description: friction between the moving fuel and the pipe builds up charge

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the purpose of the split ring commutator in a direct current motor.
parts.answer: The commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical. Without it the force on each side would reverse relative to the coil and the coil would swing back, so it would oscillate instead of turning. With it the force on each side always acts the same way round and the coil keeps rotating in one direction.
